As you are finding out, there is alot of competition when it comes to shed hunting, and few that are willing to help out when it comes to finding them. Chances are that many of the places you go to will have already had guys go through them, but they won't find them all. Some of the best advice I will give you is look on the south facing slopes. They will be snow free most of the winter, and allow the animals to stay warm, and have access to feed. Also look for mahogany trees. The big game in Utah like to spend their winters in Mahogany trees since they keep their leaves on year round. If you can find Mahogany trees on a south facing slope, you are definitely in the right spot. My favorite time of year to go is the first part of April. By then all the Moose and Deer have dropped, and elk are probably half way done. It is a great way to get exercise, and get into the great outdoors. There is enough interest these days that if you find a couple of shed antlers in a day you should consider yourself lucky. Also, the further in you go the higher your chances are of finding them. Each year you will find new spots where animals are shedding antlers. Those areas usually produce every year, so the longer you do it, the more good locations you will find, and the more productive you will become.

Best advice I've heard, and the best I can give, is focus 90% of your time searching 10% of the areas. If the spot has something going for it, grid pattern the entire spot. I think so many people think walking ten plus miles a day will yield results, when they'd be better off hitting the good spots several times over.

Another thing is to pick your spots. Spending all day walking a couple hundred acre field is frustrating and time consuming. Instead, look for specific spots that might attract deer or give deer some cover in an otherwise wide open area. I'll make sure to pick apart wet spots with reeds growing, small ditches, anything holding water, or the base of a steeper hillside. Small pockets of woods in fields are great spots. Also, while I normally don't walk many deer trails, I'll hit each one entering a field for at least fifty yards.

South facing slopes are ok, but I prefer east or southeast facing. Most of our winter days are gloomy and windy, so I feel like deer aren't as focused on basking in sunshine that doesn't exist, but rather getting out of the cold prevailing wind.

Pine trees, especially pine forest pockets can be awesome, but usually only if the pines are smaller and bunched together to create a thick canopy that will block rain and snow.

Keep in mind that I live in Ohio, so this advice might not be applicable in southern states.

Where to look depends on the terrain you have, and where you see most of the bucks in your area. Checking on farmland will be different than searching open woods or thick river bottoms.
Finding a shed is the cherry on top of a good day exploring the woods. Go slow and look hard, because they can be hard to see when standing next to one. They seem to pop out more after a rain on a cloudy day. Even when coming out empty handed, you'll have discovered a lot more in your area than you had while hunting it. Follow well run trails that have rubs. Search bedding areas if you know where they are. If not, go out when there is snow on the ground to find where the deer are bedding, and what runs they use this time of year, then return after it melts. Benches and hillsides on southern slopes usually attract deer when there is snow and/or very cold temps. Grid search spots with a lot of deer sign such as droppings and churned up leaves where they are feeding on acorns. Look in patches of cedars and pines, along roadways, pinch points, etc, where they congregate, and other places where they feed such as in briers and low lying woody browse like huckleberry and scrub oaks. Good places to go are parks closed to hunting or other sanctuaries if you have any of them around, or between houses if deer are hanging around backyards.

Some great tips offered so far, here are some thoughts...

As simple as it sounds, you have to search where the deer winter and in many cases that may not be where you hunt or even have permission to be walking. Not sure what its like near Buffalo, but in many parts trespassing can be MUCH worse in shed/morel seasons than it is in hunting season. I ran into a guy last year whose response was, "I'm not hunting"; kind of drives you crazy.

Much like hunting you'll want to focus on late season feeding and bedding areas and the travel corridors between. My focus depends on the areas I am searching...I rarely see "an antler" as much as I see a tip, or believe it or not, it is mostly the curve that catches my eye. I personally believe they are easiest to spot after a rain, when the ground is darker because it is wet. Overcast skies also help tremendously, especially if your searching cut corn and sorghum, where everything looks like an antler.

If I am on a known late season feeding area, I focus intently on the area. I have walked a cut corn field as many as 10x and found an antler on the 10th trip, that was likely there on the first, but I missed it. It takes some practice and I tell folks to bring one with you, throw it out in front of you and look to spot it as you approach. Once your eyes/brain get use to seeing them, spotting them does become a little easier.

When I have friends and family we approach areas much like a pheasant hunt and spread in straight line and search that way, yelling "bingo" if we nab one. We have two rules in groups that I organize, finders-keepers EXCEPT if a match set is found whomever found the first side gets the match from whomever found it. This has worked very well. I have had a few guys who wanted to give me the sheds they've found because they found it on my private property, I don't think that is right, they found it, but always appreciate the offer. When we hear "bingo" we will gather and start looping in concentric circles looking for the match. Two seasons ago I spent almost 15 hours over three days before I found the match to a nice 5-point side.

If I am not on a specific food source, I am on trails to and from bedding areas and IN bedding areas. I spend a lot of times at areas where trails are interrupted by fence lines, deadfalls, creeks, etc...anything that requires jumping and/or ducking under. I have some of my best success at creek and fence crossings. A few years ago, my son found this matched set about 15 feet apart, clearly could envision a buck going down the trail and bumping them off going through the deadfall....you can clearly see the well worn trail that my son is standing on and one antler at the start of where the deadfall crosses the trail and another at the other end....this areas is a well known travel corridor between a year long bedding area. This particular trail leaves an orchard and enters the thickest part of the bedding area.




Even the giant set I found in 2018 was part on the bank of a steep creek crossing...this pic doesn't do justice, although narrow the bank was more than 5' deep; when I stood in the creek, the banks were eye level. If you look close you can see the second half down the trail a bit. I could envision the buck jumping the creek, jogging the antlers loose. This trail runs for about 3/4 mile connecting a late a heavy bedding area to a late season feed source in the way of a 20acre cut corn field.



I always use the Map My Run app when I go out, turning it on when I get out of the car and off when I return. In doing so I am able to review later and see exactly where I walked and plan the next excursion, especially if I suspect there are antlers in the area. I don't mean to make it sound like a science or anything, as it is far from that, and can be a lot of fun with the right group of people. It does take A LOT of practice and patience, not only to keep your eyes down, but to keep after it. I would say I average an antler for every 5-hours or so. I think on average I cover a mile in just about an hour, sometimes longer or shorter depending on the habitat and terrain. You can search green fields like winter wheat and alfalfa with a good pair of binos. If you can use ATVs to cover ground faster, but shed hunting is definitely an activity where faster is NOT better. Go slow and if you think you're going slow enough, slow down some more. By nature our eyes are looking out in front, even up in the air, scouting for stand locations and game; its been what we've been trained to do. Like I said earlier, a great too is to bring an antler or two with you to start and toss it out in front of you every once and a while and go look for it; get your eyes used to seeing them on the ground - YES, it helps!

This season I was scouting him and knew had dropped them both about 10-days or so ago, but for one reason or the other I couldn't get out there. Go where the antlers are. Not a joke or flip response. Deer can change patterns dramatically based on feed. If they’re on the property you hunt in the winter, your odds are extremely high. As many deer herd up in winter, where you find some bone, you will usually find most. And as with anything deer, the thicker the better.

Case in point, I have a 300 acre property I hunt in Western New York and a 30 acre property I hunt in Ohio. I have shed hunted the 300 acre property for 7 years and have found literally 2 sheds putting in hundreds of hours shedding and hundreds of miles. The large property is largely high canopy open timber. The doe live there and the bucks visit in November, but there is limited agriculture. I imagine some luck SOB has a mountain of sheds from deer that Spring and Summer on neighboring properties.

The 30 acre parcel by contrast is a swamp between several ag fields. I found 3 sheds (one really nice 8 point side) in 6 months of leasing the property and I have not even had a shed season on it yet. Those sheds were found while hunting.

Long story short, it’s a needle in a haystack proposition- but you have to find the haystacks first. A property can be a bone deserts or goldmine based on known characteristics (winter deer presence and food/cover which is redundant because the deer will have a winter presence where winter food shelter is). Good to get out and exercise, but you can waste a lot of time.

Don’t over think it - it is not that difficult if you are in a good spot (again just like deer hunting).

And if your spot isn’t a shed magnet, not at all a death Nell for that piece. Just another piece of scouting info.
